Quick thoughts on Nvidia earnings…

Shared in substack chat earlier today:

A lot of people seem to think that Jensen is 100% coming back, and that Nvidia will smash results and soon erase this recent decline. I disagree. Sure, their numbers for the quarter will likely be great, as they always are, but everyone knows that already. The only thing that matters today is their guidance and the future. I think the interim CEO is going to be extremely conservative with guidance and as brief as she legally can be. Jensen was personally responsible for so many of their client deals and almost all of the circular financing that was put in place.

I also think it’s pretty clear at this point that the board doesn’t want him back, for whatever reason. I also doubt they would consider it before he testifies in front of Congress next month. There are also serious questions about the company’s Singapore/China revenue moving forward, which wasn’t pocket change. I could see an initial pop on a great quarter and misplaced hope, until those still in denial begin to accept that there is no replacing Jensen.

$NVDA earnings transcript + industry read through. To sum it up: "Demand far exceeds supply".  

- Good news for the $MU / Samsung memory longs: 

"Our supply commitments increased from $279B last quarter to $390B, primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply". (from SEC filings, not call)

This is a a major leap Q/Q in supply procurement.  

- "We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year-over-year, up from 70%." (upward revision, likely due to capacity constraints easing)

(new agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional ABF substrate capacity)

- NVIDIA said industry cloud backlog increased from $2 trillion to $2.5 trillion in a single quarter. While GPU rental pricing is continuing to rise dramatically:

Hopper GPUs: 2x their original pricing
B300 GPUs: +60% since introduction
Utilization: NVIDIA says its own compute is fully utilized across the hyperscalers and neoclouds it serves.

- "Our co-packaged optics roadmap remains on track"

Optical networking keeps growing rapidly ($21B+ in quarterly networking), CPO scale out switches has entered volume production. With Lambda earlier announcing production deployment of Nvidia photonics CPO switches. 

- "Under these agreements, we will earn revenue on the upfront sale of our infrastructure" So there's additional recurring economics coming from Neoclouds. 

But just points to industry acceleration from memory to CPO to neoclouds, relative to markets pricing in collapse.

However two things stood out:

1. Management commentary around financing: CFO said US bank financing could reach $500m, and that profits would help fund operations. CFO said share price mattered and that they'd lean more into debt.

If you look at $COHR, they fund capacity expansion from upfront prepayments. There's other ways to do it too like convertible notes.

2. Capital allocation issue: they spent $102M on three Texas buildings they had under lease. Which was around $5M annualized and I'm sure they're aware market financing conditions are tight. 

2 weeks after buying buildings when they were already relatively low on cash... AOI decided to do yet another $550M ATM. 

It's just a bit hard to justify.

Most people judge crypto payments solutions on how easy it is to spend stablecoins.

That part’s kinda solved now.

You can tap a crypto card at a restaurant and the waiter has no idea anything’s different. 

Behind that tap your money gets converted and routed so the restaurant gets paid, and you never think about it.

I wouldn’t be surprised if crypto neobanks become one of crypto’s next big product-market fits.

But what I keep thinking about is what your money’s doing the rest of the time. Like…most of it just sits there until you need to pay someone.

One project working on that is @veloprotocol, and they’re not starting from zero.

$NKE case study

One of the most important lessons I’ve learned throughout my investment career, often through my own failures trying to catch falling knives, is that you should never buy a stock simply because it has fallen significantly or because it looks cheap.

Take $NKE, for example. The business has been struggling for years, and the stock has reflected that. So why buy it?

The answer cannot simply be that it’s cheap or that it’s down 50%.

You need a reason to believe something is going to change.

Maybe you’ve visited Nike stores, studied the new product lineup, or noticed improvements that the market hasn’t fully recognized yet. Whatever it is, you need a thesis for why the future will be different from the past.

This applies to every stock.

The current price already reflects the market’s collective expectations. Your edge comes from identifying something that could change those expectations.

A stock being cheap is not an investment thesis. A stock being down 50% is not a catalyst.

You don’t buy because something has gone wrong. You buy because you have a reason to believe something is about to go right.

Podcasts, TV shows, and seemingly everyone on Wall Street and X were celebrating Leopold Aschenbrenner as the new wunderkind, the genius who had supposedly figured out Wall Street and the future of AI.

Now, with hindsight, it’s easy for everyone to see the risks. But at the time, I was almost the only voice on X warning people to be extremely careful with this guy. His returns seemed astronomical, almost illogical. Something about the numbers simply didn’t add up.

For saying that, I received countless hate messages telling me how stupid I was, that I didn’t understand his genius, and that I was simply jealous of his success. Interestingly, looking back at my original post now, I see that most of those comments have conveniently been deleted. Typical X behavior.

I’m not jealous of anyone’s success. I wish everyone great success. But one thing I’m very good at is recognizing patterns.

Only in hindsight did we discover the extraordinary leverage behind those returns. Reports indicated that his fund was borrowing as much as $3 to $4 for every $1 of capital. What appeared to be extraordinary investment genius was also extraordinary risk-taking.

According to CNBC, Aschenbrenner’s hedge fund, Situational Awareness, reached $45 billion in assets at its peak before declining to around $10 billion. Its latest 13F shows just $1.58 billion in disclosed U.S. securities, although that figure does not represent the fund’s total assets.

And this goes far beyond Aschenbrenner. Just look at the latest 13F filings. Some of the most respected hedge funds on Wall Street were loading up on AI-related stocks, including $NVDA, during the third quarter, just before the recent selloff.

These are supposed to be the smartest people in the room, surrounded by the best analysts, researchers, and resources money can buy. Yet many were heavily exposed to the very sector that subsequently collapsed.

That’s the point. Nobody has a crystal ball. There are no saviors.

There is no Wall Street genius who has cracked the market. No AI wunderkind who has discovered the secret to investing. No growth stock promoter selling you a shortcut to becoming rich.

There is a reason not everyone is wealthy. Generating exceptional investment returns consistently over long periods is extraordinarily difficult. That’s how markets work.

Never confuse a short-term track record with genuine investment skill.

Someone who wins the lottery doesn’t suddenly become the smartest person in the room. And someone who delivers three spectacular years of returns hasn’t necessarily figured out Wall Street.

Time is the ultimate test. Not podcasts, not followers, not headlines, and certainly not three years of performance.

Then Cyprus did something no country had done before. Its banks were going under, and instead of rescuing them, the authorities made the depositors pay... anything over €100,000 in your account was swapped for shares in a collapsing bank. They called it a bail-in. People lost their savings overnight.

That was the moment it dawned on me... you don’t actually own the money in your bank account. The bank does. And it can do what it likes with it.

So I went looking for somewhere to keep money that nobody else had a claim on, and that search led me to Bitcoin. I bought my first at around $200.

It started as my escape hatch from a broken banking system and eventually I understood it as the life raft out of the debasement trap.

It’s where the crypto chapter of The Everything Code picks the story up... with a generator and a cupboard full of tinned food.
